title: Your own feast days
hookLine: many Catholics keep their baptism day and their saint's name day

cards: In a Polish office in late July, someone walks in with a box of pastries, and the whole floor sings to Anna. It isn't her birthday; nobody there knows her birthday.

It's the feast of Saint Anne, and so it's her imieniny, her name day. Orthodox neighbors in Greece keep it too: the same thing can happen to a Giorgos on Saint George's day, and the phone doesn't stop ringing.
The calendar of saints walked all year isn't only the Church's calendar. In some places, it's personal.

teach.b: A name day is the feast of the saint whose name you carry.
By long custom, Catholic children were given a saint's name at baptism, and that saint became their patron: a friend in heaven, an example, someone to ask for prayers.
Church law still asks parents, godparents and the pastor not to give a name foreign to Christian sense, though it doesn't require a saint's name.
The Catechism, in paraphrase, says that in baptism the Lord's name sanctifies a person, and a Christian receives his or her own name in the Church.

teach.h: I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.
teach.b: Behind that is an old line from Isaiah, where God says to his people, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have redeemed thee, and called thee by thy name: thou art mine."
In some Catholic countries the name day is still a real celebration: Italians call it the onomastico; Poles, imieniny. Some Catholics keep a second feast: the day of their baptism.

teach.h: YOUR BAPTISM DAY, LIKE A BIRTHDAY.
teach.b: At his general audiences, Pope Francis asked people whether they knew the date of their own baptism, and suggested they find out and celebrate it like a birthday, because for Catholics that day is a kind of birth.
Some families light the baptismal candle again each year. And if your name isn't a saint's name? Catholics may take a saint's name at confirmation.
Others look for a saint from their town, or one who shared their work, or whose feast falls on their birthday. The point isn't the name itself.
It's that the great calendar of the Church has one day in it marked with your name.

how: In many Catholic countries people celebrate the feast of the saint whose name they bear, with greetings, cake or a small gift, and some families also mark each child's baptism anniversary, sometimes by lighting the baptismal candle.

games.q: your first name doesn't belong to any saint you can find. you'd still like a patron. what do Catholics often do?
o: choose a patron, often at confirmation.
go without; patrons are only for saints' names.
games.why: Catholics may take a saint's name at confirmation, or choose a patron linked to their town, their work or their birthday.

practice: Say your own first name slowly in your head, and ask whether a saint carries it, or something close.
If you know, picture that person, where they lived and what they're remembered for; if you don't, hold the question of whose name you carry, and, if you're baptized, the date it happened.
If you pray, ask your saint to pray for you.

wordCard.voice: Name day. The feast of the saint whose name you were given, kept in some Catholic countries like a second birthday. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: your own feast. Called by name, as Isaiah says, and kept on the calendar. Talk soon.
